## Exodus 17 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 — Journeying to Rephidim Without Water

- **Traditional Reading:** Israel moved "by stages" (lit. "according to their journeys," from *massa*, pulling up tent pegs) from the Wilderness of Sin. Numbers 33:12–14 fills in two omitted stations: Dophkah and Alush. They moved "according to the commandment of the LORD" — literally "at the mouth of Yahweh," signified by the movement of the pillar of cloud/fire. Yet God's direct leading brought them to Rephidim (meaning "resting places"), where there was no water. This shows that being in the centre of God's will does not exempt one from severe trials. (Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit, Guzik)  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-17.html  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/17-1.htm  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-17/

- **Geographical Note:** Rephidim is most often identified with the Wady Feiran, the most fertile valley in the Sinai Peninsula — normally watered by a copious stream, but known to dry up at times. (Pulpit, Cambridge Bible)  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/17-1.htm

- **NET Bible note:** The story is structured in three parts: the situation and complaint (vv. 1–3), the cry and miracle (vv. 4–6), and the commemoration by naming (v. 7). It intertwines God's free-flowing grace with the sad memory of Israel's sins.  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-17-commentary

---

### vv. 2–3 — The People Contend with Moses

- **Traditional Reading:** The people "contended" (Hebrew *rîb*, meaning to bring a legal case, argue, or quarrel) with Moses. They demanded water as though Moses were obliged to provide it. Their thirst was real and severe, but their response was spiritually wrong. Moses redirected the complaint: "Why do you test the LORD?" The Hebrew *nissâh* means to test or prove — they were putting God on trial, demanding He prove His presence and power. (Cambridge Bible, Ellicott, Gill)  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/17.htm  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-17.html

- **Gill notes:** The demand "Give us water" uses a plural verb, suggesting the people addressed both Moses and Aaron. They treated them "as if they were under obligation to do it for them," having seen so many miracles already.  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-17.html

- **Wiersbe:** "You never solve your problems by blaming other people. Israel's real problem was unbelief and a desire to go back to the old life. Every difficulty you meet is an opportunity for testing yourself and trusting your Lord."  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-17-commentary

- **Piper (Reformed Baptist):** The people's sin was not thirst — thirst is natural. The sin was quarrelling with Moses and testing God. Moses understood the complaint was really against the LORD.  
  (DesiringGod excerpt from search results — see search result #4, first batch)

---

### v. 4 — Moses Cries Out to the LORD

- **Traditional Reading:** Moses fled to prayer. "What shall I do with this people? A little more and they will stone me!" — this was no exaggeration. He was in a rocky valley, and stoning was the mob's natural weapon. Moses exemplified the right response to crisis: taking the problem to God rather than fighting back in the flesh. (Gill, Guzik, Pulpit)  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-17.html  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-17/

- **Kaiser (quoted by Guzik):** "One of Moses' most characteristic and praiseworthy traits was that he took his difficulties to the Lord."  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-17/

- **Gill:** Moses' cry reveals faith — not despair. He did not doubt God could help; he asked God to direct him what to do.  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-17.html

- **Piper:** God's answer to "What shall I do with this people — they are almost ready to stone me?" is simply: "I'm going to give them water." This is pure grace to the undeserving.  
  (DesiringGod excerpt from search results)

---

### vv. 5–6 — God Commands Moses to Strike the Rock

- **Traditional Reading:** God instructs Moses to (1) go ahead of the people, (2) take elders as witnesses, and (3) take the rod that struck the Nile. God promises "I will stand before you there on the rock at Horeb." The striking of the rock produced water — a miracle of both power and grace. The elders were present to verify the miracle was no natural spring. (Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit, Guzik)  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-17.html  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-17/

- **Christ Typology — Broad Protestant Consensus:** Paul explicitly identifies the rock as Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4). The rock was smitten, just as Christ was "stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted" (Isaiah 53:4). From the struck rock flowed living water, just as from Christ's riven side flowed blood and water (John 19:34). The rod of Moses represents the curse of the law; Christ bore that curse for us (Galatians 3:13). This typology is affirmed across traditions: Guzik (Pentecostal/Charismatic), Gill (Baptist), Wiersbe (Evangelical), Pulpit Commentary (Anglican), and Matthew Henry (Puritan).  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-17/  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-17-commentary  
  https://www.preceptaustin.org/moses_striking_the_rock  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/17-1.htm (Matthew Henry)

- **Gill:** The water typified "the grace of Christ, and the blessings of it, which flow from him in great abundance to the refreshment and comfort of his people, and to be had freely; and of the blood of Christ, which flowed from him when stricken and smitten."  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-17.html

- **Pulpit Commentary (Homiletics):** Notes the contrast with Numbers 20:7–12, where Moses was told only to *speak* to the rock the second time. The smiting here was significant — it was "an act of violence" opening the way for water, picturing the cross.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/exodus/17.htm

- **Distinction — Kadesh vs. Rephidim:** At Rephidim (Exodus 17), the rock was to be *struck* — picturing Christ's first coming and crucifixion. At Kadesh (Numbers 20), the rock was only to be *spoken to* — picturing access to Christ through prayer after His once-for-all sacrifice. Moses' failure at Kadesh (striking the rock twice) marred the type. This distinction is widely noted in conservative Protestant teaching. (Pulpit, Wiersbe)  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/exodus/17.htm

- **Piper (Reformed Baptist):** Emphasises four aspects of God's grace in this miracle: (1) God gives water to undeserving grumblers; (2) the miracle is public before elders; (3) it continues the power demonstrated in the plagues — same rod, same God; (4) most wonderfully, God says "I will stand before you on the rock" — His presence is the best gift.  
  (DesiringGod excerpt from search results)

---

### v. 7 — Massah and Meribah

- **Traditional Reading:** *Massah* means "testing" or "proving" (from *nissâh*); *Meribah* means "strife" or "quarrel" (from *rîb*). The name memorialised not God's mercy but Israel's sin. "Is the LORD among us or not?" was their great failure — doubting the presence of the God who had visibly led them by cloud and fire and now promised to stand on the rock before Moses. (Cambridge Bible, Ellicott, Gill, Guzik)  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/exodus/17.htm  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-17.html

- **Piper:** The story deliberately ends on a note of failure — Israel's failure, not God's. Moses doesn't name the place "Grace Abounding" or "Water from the Rock"; he names it "Testing and Quarrelling." The Bible repeatedly warns against imitating this unbelief (Psalm 95:7–9; Hebrews 3:7–11).  
  (DesiringGod excerpt from search results)

- **Dr. Constable (Evangelical):** "Massah" means "testing" or "proof," and "Meribah" means "murmuring," "dissatisfaction," or "contention." They failed to believe the Lord was among them as He had promised.  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/exodus-17.html

---

### vv. 8–9 — Amalek Attacks; Joshua Commissioned

- **Traditional Reading:** This was an unprovoked attack. Amalek was descended from Esau (Genesis 36:12), making them distant kin to Israel. Deuteronomy 25:17–18 reveals the cowardly nature of the attack: they struck the rear ranks — the tired, the stragglers, the weak. This is the first mention of Joshua (whose name in Greek is "Jesus"). Moses commissioned him to choose men and fight, while Moses would ascend the hill with "the rod of God." (Clarke, Gill, Guzik)  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-17/  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-17.html

- **Clarke:** "Both in the Septuagint and Greek Testament he is called Jesus: the name signifies Saviour; and he is allowed to have been a very expressive type of our blessed Lord."  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-17/

- **Gill:** The rod was the same rod of miracles. Moses held it "as a banner" so the army could see it and be encouraged that God was with them.  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-17.html

- **Morgan (quoted by Guzik):** "In their first movement God led them in such a way as to avoid the possibility of war (Exodus 13:17). Now they were involved in war." God was teaching them a new lesson: fighting with divine dependence.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-17/

---

### vv. 10–11 — Moses' Hands: Israel Prevails or Falters

- **Traditional Reading:** As long as Moses held up his hands (with the rod), Israel prevailed; when his hands dropped, Amalek prevailed. The almost universal interpretation — from the Targums, Rabbis, Church Fathers, Reformers, and modern commentators — is that Moses was engaged in intercessory prayer. The lifting of hands was the ancient Israelite posture of prayer (cf. Psalm 28:2, 63:4; 1 Timothy 2:8). (Keil & Delitzsch, Clarke, Guzik)  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/17-11.html  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-17/

- **Alternate View — Ensign/Banner:** Some commentators (notably JFB and Cambridge) suggest the lifted hands were primarily a visible sign to the troops — like a battle-standard — rather than (or in addition to) prayer. The rod lifted high served as a rallying banner. Both the prayer and banner interpretations are widely held and not seen as contradictory.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/exodus/17-11.htm  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/17-11.html

- **Clarke:** "We cannot understand this transaction in any literal way; for the lifting up or letting down the hands of Moses could not, humanly speaking, influence the battle. It is likely that he held up the rod of God … as an ensign to the people." The Jerusalem Targum explicitly says, "When Moses held up his hands in prayer, the house of Israel prevailed."  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/17-11.html

- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** "So mighty was the prayer of Moses that all depended upon it. The petitions of Moses discomfited the enemy more than the fighting of Joshua. The edge of Moses' prayer was more powerful than the edge of Joshua's sword." Yet Spurgeon also insists: prayer without action is mockery — "Prayer is a downright mockery if it does not lead us into the practical use of means likely to promote the ends for which we pray."  
  https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/war-with-amalek  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-17/

- **Church Fathers' View:** "Several of the fathers consider Moses, with his stretched-out hands, as a figure of Christ on the cross, suffering for mankind, and getting a complete victory over sin and Satan." (Clarke, cited by Guzik)  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-17/

- **Keil & Delitzsch:** The lifting up of the staff secured divine strength for the warriors. "There is no other way in which we can explain the effect produced upon the battle … God had not promised him miraculous help for the conflict … for this reason he lifted up his hands with the staff in prayer to God."  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/exodus/17-11.html

---

### vv. 12–13 — Aaron and Hur Support Moses' Hands

- **Traditional Reading:** Moses' hands grew heavy — prayer is hard work. Aaron and Hur placed a stone under him and held up his hands, one on each side, until sunset. This shows the necessity of community in spiritual warfare: even the greatest intercessor cannot sustain the work alone. Joshua defeated Amalek with the sword — human effort and divine power cooperated. (Guzik, Spurgeon, Gill)  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-17/

- **Spurgeon:** "It is far easier to fight with sin in public, than to pray against it in private. … Joshua never grew weary in the fighting, but Moses did grow weary in the praying; the more spiritual an exercise, the more difficult it is for flesh and blood to maintain it."  
  https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/war-with-amalek

- **Guzik (Pentecostal/Charismatic):** "We are left with no other option than to say if Moses, Aaron, and Hur did not do the work in prayer, Israel would have been defeated, and history would have been changed."  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-17/

- **On Hur:** Jewish tradition (Josephus, *Antiquities* III, 54) identifies Hur as the husband of Miriam, Moses' sister. (Kaiser, cited by Guzik)  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-17/

---

### vv. 14–16 — The Book of Remembrance, Yahweh-Nissi, and Perpetual War

- **Traditional Reading (v. 14):** God commands Moses to write the account "in the book" (*bassēfer*) as a memorial. This is one of five places in the Pentateuch where Moses is commanded to write (also Exodus 24:4–7; 34:27; Numbers 33:1–2; Deuteronomy 31:9, 24). God promises to "utterly blot out the remembrance of Amalek from under heaven." (Kaiser, cited by Guzik)  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-17/

- **Traditional Reading (v. 15):** Moses built an altar and named it **Yahweh-Nissi** ("The LORD Is My Banner"). A *nēs* is a flag or standard raised high in battle. The same word is used for the bronze serpent on the pole (Numbers 21:8) and for the Root of Jesse who stands as a banner for the peoples (Isaiah 11:10). The name gives all glory to God, not to Moses' prayer or Joshua's sword. (Guzik, Gill)  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-17/  
  https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/exodus-17.html

- **Traditional Reading (v. 16):** "A hand was lifted up toward the throne of the LORD" (or "Because the LORD has sworn"). The Hebrew is difficult; some translations read "a hand upon the throne of the LORD" (ESV margin) or "the LORD has sworn." The sense is that the LORD will be at war with Amalek from generation to generation. (Cambridge Bible, Guzik)  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-17/

- **Amalek in Redemptive History:** Amalek's doom unfolds across Scripture: Balaam's prophecy (Numbers 24:20), Saul's partial obedience (1 Samuel 15, which cost him the throne), David's campaigns (1 Samuel 30; 2 Samuel 8:12), and the apparent completion under Hezekiah (1 Chronicles 4:41–43). Yet Haman the Agagite (Esther 3:1) may represent a surviving Amalekite line. (Guzik)  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-17/

- **Amalek as a Type of the Flesh:** Many evangelical teachers (including Guzik) note that Amalek is widely seen as a picture of the flesh — the unspiritual nature that wars against the spirit (Galatians 5:17). Just as God declared perpetual war on Amalek, so the believer must wage unceasing war against indwelling sin.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-17/

- **Spurgeon:** "You must wrestle with your sin, but the major part of the wrestling must be done alone in private with God. … It is not praying today nor yet tomorrow that will win life's battle, it is praying till the going down of the sun … till the evening of life is over."  
  https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/war-with-amalek

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

**On the whole, Exodus 17 is not a chapter where major Protestant traditions sharply divide.** The typology of Christ the Rock (1 Corinthians 10:4) is universally affirmed. The main differences are of emphasis:

- **Reformed / Piper:** Stresses God's sovereign, gracious provision to utterly undeserving grumblers. The emphasis falls on God's free grace, not human effort. The naming of Massah and Meribah highlights the sin of unbelief.  
  (DesiringGod excerpt from search results)

- **Baptist / Spurgeon:** Strongly emphasises the necessity of both prayer *and* action working together — "hard blows and hard prayers." Prayer alone is not enough; neither is fighting alone. Also stresses perseverance in prayer until the end of life.  
  https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/war-with-amalek  
  https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/the-war-of-truth

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic / Guzik (Enduring Word):** Emphasises that "life or death for Israel depended on the prayers of one man" and that the real battle is won through intercession. The hands-lifted posture is identified without hesitation as prayer. Strong emphasis on the continuing power of intercessory prayer to change outcomes.  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/exodus-17/

- **Anglican / Pulpit Commentary:** Gives careful attention to the two rock-striking events (Exodus 17 vs. Numbers 20), noting the theological significance of smiting vs. speaking. Also emphasises the sacramental and homiletic dimensions — the water as "spiritual drink" and the rock as Christ.  
  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/exodus/17.htm

- **Lutheran:** No specific Lutheran commentary on Exodus 17 was found on lcms.org or 1517.org in the searches performed.

- **Methodist/Wesleyan:** No specific Wesleyan commentary on Exodus 17 was found on seedbed.com or wesley.nnu.edu in the searches performed.

## Other Views

**Modern Scholarship (NET Bible notes, accessed via Precept Austin):**  
The narrative is analysed as an intertwining of God's grace and Israel's sin. The passage is structured in three movements: complaint (vv. 1–3), miracle (vv. 4–6), commemoration (v. 7). The story serves an important theological point in Exodus: God can give water where none is available. The narrative foregrounds Israel's striving but is fundamentally about God's free-flowing grace.  
https://www.preceptaustin.org/exodus-17-commentary

**Catholic and Orthodox Readings:** No results were returned from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org in the searches performed.

**Debated Popular Modern Teaching:** No specific prosperity, Word of Faith, or hyper-grace teaching on Exodus 17 was found in the searches performed.

## Summary of Key Themes Across All Traditions

1. **Testing in the Will of God:** Rephidim means "resting places," yet it brought thirst. God leads His people into difficulty to teach dependence.
2. **Christ the Smitten Rock:** The rock is a clear type of Christ, struck for our sins, from whom flows living water — the Holy Spirit (1 Cor 10:4; John 7:37–39).
3. **The Sin of Unbelief:** The great sin at Massah and Meribah was doubting God's presence: "Is the LORD among us or not?" This is repeatedly warned against in Scripture (Psalm 95; Hebrews 3–4).
4. **Prayer and Action Together:** The battle was won on the hilltop through intercession *and* in the valley through the sword. Neither replaces the other.
5. **The Fellowship of Intercession:** Aaron and Hur holding up Moses' hands pictures the church's calling to support its leaders and one another in prayer.
6. **Yahweh-Nissi:** The LORD is our banner — victory belongs to God alone, and the glory goes to Him.
